summary: A list of RFCs by number, dated August 1, 1971, giving each document's first author, title, date and NIC and RFC numbers. It extends earlier lists such as RFC 170 and RFC 160 and was a tool for finding documents.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of all the notes so far, in number order, with who wrote each. It helps you find the one you need.

questions: where is a list of rfcs by number
what did the rfc list of august 1971 contain
what is a nic number in old rfcs
subtitle: A 1971 index of the first 200 RFCs, listing author, title, date and NIC number for each.

tldr.problem: By August 1971 the Network Working Group had circulated hundreds of notes, and people needed a way to find the one they wanted.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 200 is a single table in RFC number order. Each row gives the first author, the title, the date, the NIC number and the RFC number.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the earlier list in RFC 170 (and RFC 160, a brief list by title), and it records the whole run of notes from RFC 1 of April 1969 to RFC 200 itself.

today: The metadata gives no standards status for RFC 200. It obsoletes RFC 160 and RFC 170 and is itself a historical snapshot of the series as of August 1971.

sections.title: What the List Is
sections.content:
RFC 200 is titled RFC List by Number. It is dated August 1, 1971, carries NIC number 7152 and gives the author as unknown. It has no prose: the whole document is a table.

It obsoletes the earlier lists in RFC 160 and RFC 170. The list itself is entered as the last row, RFC 200 dated 1 August 1971.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a long table, with no story, that lists every note written so far.

sections.title: The Columns
sections.content:
Each row has five pieces of information: the first author (by surname, with a few rows naming a group such as NIC), the title, the date, the NIC number and the RFC number. Long titles wrap onto a second line.

The NIC number is a separate catalogue number. It is not the same as the RFC number, and the list shows both side by side, for example NIC 4687 for RFC 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line says who wrote the note, what it is called, when it was written, and two numbers you can use to ask for it.

sections.title: What It Records
sections.content:
The list starts with RFC 1, "HOST Software" by Crocker, dated 7 April 1969. It then runs through topics such as host software, the HOST-IMP interface, TELNET, file transfer, remote job entry and network graphics. For instance it lists RFC 114, "A File Transfer Protocol", of 16 April 1971.

Not every number was used. Some rows are marked "no RFC by this number ever issued", for example for numbers 14, 92 and 159. A few entries are revisions: RFC 137 appears twice, the second time marked "rev". The last lines record that the text was put into machine readable form for the online archives in March 1998.
sections.plainLanguage: You can see the early network community at work: who was writing, on which subjects, and the odd gap where a number was skipped.
